group.passage: Before the French Revolution, a trader moving from town to town could find that familiar units had quietly changed. The country used hundreds of different measures, and even units with the same name did not agree. A pinte of wine, for example, held 0.93 liters in Paris but 1.46 liters in Saint-Denis, a town just to the north. Such confusion made cheating easy and slowed down trade. After the revolution began, French scientists were asked to create one system for the whole nation. Rather than simply adopt the measures of Paris, which they considered arbitrary, they turned to nature. In 1791 they proposed that a new unit, the metre, should equal one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. Because such a length belonged to the planet rather than to any town or king, they hoped other countries would accept it as well. Nobody could walk from the pole to the equator, of course, so the plan was to measure one slice of that line and work out the rest. In 1792 two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, set out to survey the stretch from Dunkirk on the northern coast through Paris to Barcelona in Spain. They measured angles between survey stations, some on mountain tops, and turned the angles into distances. The work was slow and risky: France was in the middle of a revolution, and in 1793 a war with Spain stopped Méchain’s work in Barcelona. Méchain also carried a secret. He had noticed that two sets of his readings for Barcelona did not match, and, afraid of being blamed, he told no one and later changed some figures. Delambre discovered this only after Méchain’s death, but by then the metre was already law, so he kept quiet. The fieldwork ended in 1798, and the next year a platinum bar was made as the official metre. It was about 0.2 millimeters shorter than planned. Even then, many French people held on to their old units, and the metric system was not firmly restored in France until 1837. Since 1983, the metre has been defined not by the Earth but by light: it is the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

translation_zh.text:
公尺是怎麼來的

法國大革命之前，一個從一座城鎮走到另一座城鎮的商人，可能會發現熟悉的單位悄悄變了。全國使用數百種不同的量度，就連名稱相同的單位也互不一致。舉例來說，一「品脫」（pinte）的酒在巴黎是 0.93 公升，在北邊不遠的聖但尼（Saint-Denis）卻是 1.46 公升。這樣的混亂讓人很容易作弊，也拖慢了貿易。

大革命開始後，法國科學家奉命替全國建立一套統一的制度。他們認為巴黎的量度太過武斷，不願直接沿用，而是轉向大自然。1791 年，他們提議一個新單位「公尺」應該等於北極到赤道距離的一千萬分之一。由於這樣的長度屬於整個地球，而不屬於任何城鎮或國王，他們希望其他國家也會接受它。

當然，沒有人能從北極走到赤道，所以計畫是測量這條線的其中一段，其餘再推算出來。1792 年，兩位天文學家德朗布爾（Jean-Baptiste Delambre）與梅尚（Pierre Méchain）出發，測量從北部海岸的敦克爾克經過巴黎、一直到西班牙巴塞隆納的這一段。他們測量各測站之間的角度（有些測站設在山頂上），再把角度換算成距離。這項工作緩慢又危險：法國正處於革命之中，而 1793 年與西班牙之間的戰爭讓梅尚在巴塞隆納的工作中斷了。

梅尚還背負著一個秘密。他發現自己在巴塞隆納測得的兩組讀數對不上，又怕被責怪，於是沒有告訴任何人，後來還改了一些數字。德朗布爾直到梅尚過世後才發現這件事，但當時公尺已經成為法律，所以他保持沉默。實地測量在 1798 年結束，隔年製成一根鉑金尺作為官方的公尺。它比預定的長度短了大約 0.2 毫米。

即使如此，許多法國人仍沿用舊的單位，公制直到 1837 年才在法國穩固地恢復。自 1983 年起，公尺不再以地球、而是以光來定義：它是光在真空中於 1/299,792,458 秒內行進的距離。

open_tasks.prompt: The French scientists hoped that a unit based on the Earth would be accepted by every country. Do you think basing the metre on nature was a good idea? Give one reason in one or two English sentences.
reference_answers: Yes, because a unit taken from the Earth belongs to no single king or town, so other countries could accept it without feeling that they were following France.
It was a good idea at first, but measuring the Earth was so hard that the result was a little off, so tying the metre to light later made more sense.
